## Decision summary

**Keep flat supervised execution as the default. The external evidence supports bounded specialist delegation, but does not establish that adding a supervised middle layer will improve this repository’s outcomes.** Its strongest potential value is local decomposition when a worker discovers independently executable work that could not reasonably have been assigned beforehand. Its principal additional costs are another decision-making and monitoring loop, another context boundary, and responsibility for the lifetime and outcomes of a subtree. This is a decision synthesis, not a measured result or permission to change the current contract. Sources: [Anthropic’s research-system report](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), [building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents), [Erlang supervision](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html), and [MAST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the cited primary descriptions; MEDIUM for transfer to this repository. Relationship: supports current caution and extends the decision criteria.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Three distinctions control the conclusion:

1. **Parallel workers do not require nested supervisors.** Anthropic’s reported research architecture already parallelizes multiple workers under one lead; it is not evidence for a second coordinating generation. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance: HIGH; reliability: HIGH, first-party engineering account; relationship: supports the flat baseline.**  
   <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->
2. **A hierarchy of tasks or contexts is not automatically a hierarchy of authority or recovery.** LangGraph and AutoGen demonstrate composition and encapsulation; Erlang specifies lifecycle supervision. None supplies this repository’s human-approval, publication, or worker-contract policy. [LangGraph](https://www.langchain.com/blog/langgraph-multi-agent-workflows), [AutoGen 0.2](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/tutorial/conversation-patterns/), [Erlang](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). **Relevance: HIGH; reliability: HIGH for documented mechanisms; relationship: extends the distinction between launch ancestry and supervision.**  
   <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->
3. **Current web documentation must replace remembered product limitations.** The retrieved Claude Code documentation explicitly permits nested subagents by default. That does not establish the installed harness’s behavior, alter Orca’s separate depth rules, or repeal the local worker ban. [Source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). **Relevance: HIGH; reliability: HIGH for current published documentation, UNVERIFIED for the installed runtime; relationship: contradicts an outdated blanket “Claude subagents cannot nest” argument, not the local contract.**  
   <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## Method, provenance, and evidence boundaries

- Read the exact assigned prompt and ensuring clauses before researching.
- Read the assigned research summaries, research-05’s correction addendum, and the current gaps register. Earlier broad summaries were not treated as controlling.
- Tavily search/extract tools, including callable aliases, were absent from this agent’s available tool surface. Therefore the permitted **`tavily-unavailable`** fallback applied. WebSearch discovered sources; WebFetch inspected their contents. Each external finding below carries the required fallback annotation.
- External queries used generic public concepts only. No private repository content, internal issue text, or local source was submitted to external services.
- Official documentation and original papers were preferred. Vendor engineering reports were treated as evidence about their reported systems, not independent proof that their architecture transfers.
- Framework examples were distinguished from controlled comparisons. Unpinned live documentation was not assigned an invented package version.
- **[CODE-VERIFIED] below means directly inspected source or shipped instructions, not demonstrated runtime success.** Reading a Markdown rule verifies that the instruction exists; it does not prove universal compliance.

### Comparison terminology

For this report:

- **Flat supervised:** one coordinator directly delegates to workers.
- **Hierarchical supervised:** an upper coordinator delegates to a middle session that itself coordinates lower workers and reports upward.
- **Peer/networked:** workers may communicate or hand control among peers.
- **Single-agent:** one agent does the work without delegated workers.

These are analytical definitions. In particular, a multi-agent-versus-single-agent result is **not** a hierarchy-versus-flat result.

## 1. Anthropic: demonstrated benefits are workload-specific

### F1. Breadth-first research can benefit from one lead with independent workers

Anthropic describes a lead agent that plans, delegates independent investigations, evaluates returned findings, and synthesizes them. Separate worker contexts support independent exploration and compression. This is direct evidence for **one lead with parallel workers**, not for recursively nested managers. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for its own architecture; MEDIUM for comparative claims outside its evaluation. Relationship: supports flat specialist fan-out and extends context-management options.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The authors identify extensive shared context and tightly coupled dependencies as poorer fits, noting that many coding tasks offer less independent parallel work than research. Consequently, “multi-agent research worked” does not establish that concurrent code-writing subtrees will integrate correctly. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, qualified first-party observation. Relationship: supports existing write isolation and bounded delegation.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F2. Explicit briefs and artifact references matter more than labels

Anthropic reports that vague assignments led to overlapping searches, gaps, and inconsistent interpretations. Worker briefs should identify the objective, deliverable, relevant tools/sources, and boundaries. For suitable outputs, workers can persist artifacts and return references rather than pass the complete content through the lead, reducing repeated transfer and information degradation. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for observed engineering problems; no isolated effect size. Relationship: supports explicit local briefs and artifact admission; extends the case for preserving evidence below summaries.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The same report describes overspawning, excessive updates, searches continuing after sufficient evidence, and downstream behavioral changes from small prompt/tool changes. More agents therefore create more opportunities for waste and coordination failure unless the work is bounded. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, first-party operational account. Relationship: supports fan-out and lineage-budget concerns.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F3. Parallelism does not remove synchronization overhead

The reported research system has a synchronous batch boundary: the lead waits for its worker group, cannot redirect active workers, and can be delayed by one slow worker. The authors discuss asynchronous operation as a future improvement that also introduces result reconciliation, consistency, and failure-propagation difficulties. They do not report a measured asynchronous improvement. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the described system. Relationship: extends latency, blocked-parent, and ownership questions.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F4. Dynamic decomposition has a narrower justification than “large task”

Anthropic’s broader guidance distinguishes predefined workflows, parallel independent work, and an orchestrator that dynamically determines subtasks. It recommends the simplest adequate approach and adding complexity when evaluation demonstrates value. Dynamic decomposition is useful when the required subtasks cannot reasonably be specified in advance; fixed independent assignments do not inherently require another model-directed manager. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official architectural guidance rather than a controlled topology experiment. Relationship: supports D5’s runtime-only split criterion.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 2. Claude Code subagents: context isolation has both benefits and costs

### F5. Fresh contexts trade parent-context savings for delegation and reconstruction work

The retrieved documentation says ordinary subagents start with fresh isolated context; the parent composes a delegation message, and the subagent returns a summary. A fork instead inherits the parent conversation. Subagent requests count against shared usage limits, returned detail still consumes parent context, and fresh subagents may need time to gather context. [Source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for published product behavior; installed behavior UNVERIFIED. Relationship: supports bounded local helpers and extends cost/context-loss analysis.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The documentation recommends the main conversation when phases share substantial context, require frequent back-and-forth, or are latency-sensitive; subagents fit self-contained work whose verbose exploration need not remain in the parent context. Therefore context isolation is a trade, not proof of lower total tokens or lower latency. [Source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official guidance; no universal numerical effect. Relationship: supports choosing delegation by task shape.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F6. Current documentation explicitly supports nesting

Under “Let subagents spawn their own subagents,” the retrieved page states:

> “By default, a subagent can spawn subagents of its own, up to three layers below the main conversation.”

It describes depth-dependent withholding of the Agent tool, with a fork exception in tool visibility but an error when spawning at the limit. The page also describes a separate default concurrent limit of 20, with exceptions, and identifies that concurrency feature as requiring Claude Code v2.1.217 or later. The nesting section itself does not provide an introduction version. [Source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the retrieved documentation; installed applicability UNVERIFIED. Relationship: contradicts an outdated universal no-nesting premise, while leaving Orca policy unchanged.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The page further documents environment-dependent waiting: with fork mode off in print/SDK use, a nested background agent may outlast its spawning subagent and report to the main conversation. **Inference:** completion and ownership cannot safely be deduced merely from the visual nesting of a call. This is not evidence about Orca’s runtime. [Source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for documented behavior; MEDIUM for the lifecycle inference. Relationship: extends the parent-exit/orphan question.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 3. Erlang/OTP: a strong lifecycle analogy, not an LLM benchmark

### F7. Supervision trees make failure policy explicit

OTP supervisors can supervise workers or other supervisors. The documented restart strategies distinguish restarting one child, restarting the entire sibling group, and restarting the failed child plus later-started dependents. Startup normally follows specification order and shutdown reverses it. [Source](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). **Relevance: HIGH for lifecycle design, MEDIUM for LLM architecture. Reliability: HIGH, official runtime documentation. Relationship: extends cancellation, dependency, and failure-domain questions.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Inference for this decision:** a useful middle supervisor must own an explicit failure policy, not merely relay messages. “Restart the child,” “fail the group,” and “continue with partial results” are materially different outcomes. OTP’s supervision does not verify semantic correctness, restore human authority, or make a repeated external side effect safe. [Source](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the mechanism; MEDIUM for transfer. Relationship: extends the local aggregate-outcome and recovery requirements.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F8. Nested retry allowances multiply

The OTP documentation explicitly warns that restart intensities multiply across supervisor levels: allowances of 10 at two levels can permit 100 worker restarts. It recommends much smaller upper-level allowances in that example, at most three. These numbers describe OTP’s example—not an appropriate retry allowance for LLM workers. [Source](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documented arithmetic. Relationship: supports budgets that account for the entire lineage rather than resetting at each manager.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F9. Shutdown and upward requests can deadlock or strand descendants

OTP warns that finite shutdown timeouts for supervisor children can kill them before descendant termination finishes; unlimited worker cleanup can instead hang indefinitely. It also describes a deadlock when a worker synchronously asks an ancestor to terminate its subtree while that ancestor waits for the worker to exit. [Source](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for OTP behavior; MEDIUM as an LLM-system analogy. Relationship: extends blocked-parent, cancellation, and subtree-quiescence concerns.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Decision implication:** “parent stopped” must not be treated as “subtree stopped.” This is a design inference, not a claim that the repository has an OTP-style deadlock. [Source](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM, explicitly bounded analogy. Relationship: extends recovery criteria without overriding current code.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 4. LangGraph: hierarchy is composable, but context boundaries remain a design choice

### F10. The official examples distinguish shared history, separate workers, and nested teams

LangChain’s January 2024 explanation distinguishes:

- collaboration through a shared scratchpad;
- a supervisor coordinating workers with their own histories, adding completed outputs to shared history;
- hierarchical teams in which a LangGraph graph is itself a node in another graph.

This demonstrates architectural composition, not measured superiority. The article provides no controlled latency, cost, or accuracy comparison. [Source](https://www.langchain.com/blog/langgraph-multi-agent-workflows). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for its historical architecture description; MEDIUM for current API applicability. Relationship: extends the available conceptual options.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F11. Full history and final-message handoffs solve different problems

The supervisor repository documents higher-level supervisors over compiled research/writing teams. It also distinguishes retaining a worker’s full history from retaining only its last message. Default delegation history and returned worker history are separate controls; custom handoff tools can choose what information a worker receives, and a forwarding tool can avoid supervisor paraphrasing of a worker’s final response. [Source](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the repository’s documented behavior; MEDIUM for new adoption. Relationship: extends context-loss and evidence-preservation choices.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The retrieved repository page is archived/read-only and its README recommends a directly implemented tool-calling supervisor for most new uses because it offers greater context-engineering control. This is not a recommendation to add that package here. Its in-memory checkpoint examples also do not establish durable recovery. [Source](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py). **Relevance: MEDIUM. Reliability: HIGH for repository status and README contents. Relationship: supports avoiding a framework choice before the decision is justified.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Current subagent guidance likewise distinguishes fresh per-invocation execution from persistent specialist history, and blocking calls from background jobs requiring job/status/result infrastructure. It documents qualitative costs such as repeated work, larger inherited prompts, and background-job complexity, but supplies no comparative performance measurements. [Source](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/multi-agent/subagents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: extends the context-versus-continuity and monitoring tradeoffs.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### Source-verification limitation: the old notebook is not current implementation evidence

The repository’s main-branch example notebook is a moved-file stub. Its pinned historical replacement could only be partially inspected through WebFetch because embedded image content dominated the extraction. The readable tail showed a stream invocation with a recursion limit of 150, but did not establish the supervisor or context-adapter definitions. No claims about those unobserved definitions are used here. [Stub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/main/examples/multi_agent/hierarchical_agent_teams.ipynb), [pinned historical notebook](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/23961cff61a42b52525f3b20b4094d8d2fba1744/docs/docs/tutorials/multi_agent/hierarchical_agent_teams.ipynb). **Relevance: MEDIUM. Reliability: HIGH for the observed artifact contents; implementation details UNVERIFIED. Relationship: prevents stale-example generalization.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 5. AutoGen nested chats: encapsulation and local limits are not a subtree budget

### F12. Nested conversations provide one outward-facing interface

AutoGen **0.2** documents an agent that initiates internal conversations and returns a summary to its caller. Nested conversations can include individual agents or group chats. Summaries accumulate as carryover; by default the enclosing response uses the final nested chat’s summary. The example excludes internal participants from the trigger to avoid recursive activation. [Source](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/tutorial/conversation-patterns/). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for versioned official examples; not a current-version API claim. Relationship: extends the composite-task interface and context-loss analysis.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F13. Per-conversation bounds do not establish an aggregate resource ceiling

The tutorial distinguishes `max_turns` for a two-agent conversation from `max_round` for a group conversation. Those bounds operate at different scopes; they are not a single end-to-end allowance for every nested conversation. Selecting a last-message summary is also different from requesting an LLM-generated summary. [Source](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/tutorial/conversation-patterns/). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, versioned documentation. Relationship: supports explicit whole-task budgeting and output contracts.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The tutorial includes toy arithmetic and code-verification examples, plus example token/cost output, but no controlled nesting-versus-flat comparison or latency study. Some demonstrated conversations stop without reaching the requested target. Examples therefore show mechanisms, not general reliability. [Source](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/0.2/docs/tutorial/conversation-patterns/). **Relevance: MEDIUM. Reliability: HIGH for shown examples; LOW as comparative performance evidence. Relationship: supports cautious interpretation of framework tutorials.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 6. CrewAI hierarchy: managerial routing does not imply parallel execution

### F14. Managerial assignment and validation are documented capabilities

CrewAI documents sequential and hierarchical processes. In hierarchy, a manager assigns work according to capabilities, checks results, and determines completion. A hierarchy requires an automatically powered manager or a supplied custom manager. The guides discuss context-window handling, optional planning, request-rate limits, and iteration limits. [Hierarchical process](https://docs.crewai.com/en/learn/hierarchical-process), [process definitions](https://docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/processes). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for official feature descriptions. Relationship: extends possible middle-role responsibilities.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Neither inspected page establishes that managerial delegation executes concurrently or provides measured accuracy, token, cost, or latency improvements over sequential/flat alternatives. The advertised efficiency and coordination benefits must not be reported as benchmark results. The pages also do not demonstrate a shared monetary or aggregate-token ceiling across a subtree. [Hierarchical process](https://docs.crewai.com/en/learn/hierarchical-process), [process definitions](https://docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/processes). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the evidence limitation in those pages. Relationship: supports separating hierarchy, parallelism, and budgeting.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 7. Credible critiques: fragmented decisions and verification failures

### F15. Cognition’s original critique concerns missing decision context

Cognition’s June 2025 critique argues that task descriptions or selected messages may omit consequential decisions carried in full interaction traces. Parallel coding agents can make incompatible choices even when they start from the same information. It favors continuous context for coupled work while acknowledging bounded investigative delegation. The article provides illustrative engineering arguments, not a controlled universal failure rate. [Source](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM, first-party practitioner analysis rather than a controlled study. Relationship: supports caution about parallel writers and extends context-loss concerns.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F16. The later critique supports narrower collaboration, not an absolute ban

Cognition’s April 2026 follow-up reports useful author–reviewer loops, expert consultation, and hierarchical coordination, while continuing to warn about fragmented decisions and conflicting concurrent modifications. It explicitly describes information sharing and delegation granularity as unfinished problems. Thus the earlier title should not be used as a timeless rejection of all multi-agent designs. [Source](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM, first-party operational report. Relationship: extends the options beyond “single agent or unrestricted swarm.”**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The follow-up does not discuss parallel Git worktrees. **Inference:** workspace isolation can prevent direct file interference without necessarily preventing conflicting assumptions or expensive integration. That inference is consistent with the critique but is not a measured worktree result. [Source](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: MEDIUM for the inference. Relationship: supports retaining both write isolation and explicit admission/integration ownership.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### F17. MAST identifies concrete failure categories, not a winning topology

The latest retrieved version of **“Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?”** is v3, revised October 26, 2025. It introduces 14 failure modes across system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification, with more than 1,600 traces across seven frameworks. Relevant modes include repeated work, context loss, unclear stopping conditions, failure to request clarification, withholding relevant information, premature termination, and defective verification. [Abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657), [full paper v3](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, primary research; transfer limited by evaluated systems and annotation method. Relationship: supports the gap register’s reporting, stopping, and verification concerns.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Most corpus labels were machine-produced, with much smaller expert-annotated development/validation sets. Observed failure categories are not independent per-task probabilities, and framework/model/benchmark differences do not isolate the effect of hierarchy. The inspected paper contains no explicitly designated, controlled hierarchy-versus-flat experiment. [Source](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for methodology and scope. Relationship: prevents causal overstatement.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

Its interventions reinforce explicit termination authority and high-level goal verification, but the results depend on model and benchmark. **Inference:** adding a manager without specifying completion and verification can relocate errors rather than remove them. [Source](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for reported interventions; MEDIUM for the inference. Relationship: extends aggregate-admission and completion criteria.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 8. Quantitative evidence and limits

| Reported observation | Correct interpretation | What it does **not** establish |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic reports **90.2% outperformance** for an Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 workers versus single-agent Opus 4 on its internal research evaluation | A task- and model-specific comparison reported by the vendor; the article does not provide underlying scores sufficient to restate it as percentage-point accuracy | No depth-2-versus-flat benefit; no repository-specific gain. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance HIGH; reliability HIGH for reported result, MEDIUM for transfer; relationship extends value evidence.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> |
| Approximately **4×** tokens for agents and **15×** for multi-agent systems | Both use ordinary chats as the stated baseline | Not a 15× comparison against single-agent research; not a dollar-cost multiplier; not a hierarchy penalty. [Source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). **Relevance HIGH; reliability HIGH/observational; relationship extends cost caution.** <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable --> |
